title: Binary Tree Traversal (In/Pre/Post)
directAnswer: Visit every node in a fixed order. Preorder = node, left, right; inorder = left, node, right; postorder = left, right, node. The recursive form is three lines — just move the `visit(node)` call relative to the two recursive calls. The interview-grade follow-up is the iterative inorder using an explicit stack (O(h) space), and the brag-worthy O(1)-space answer is Morris traversal via threaded links.

remember.pattern: Depth-first tree walk (pre/in/post) + explicit-stack iterative variant
remember.formula:
preorder:  visit(node); dfs(left); dfs(right)
inorder:   dfs(left); visit(node); dfs(right)
postorder: dfs(left); dfs(right); visit(node)
rules: The **only** difference between the three orders is *where* you place the `visit(node)` line relative to the two recursive calls.
**Inorder of a BST is sorted** — this single fact powers Validate BST, Kth Smallest, and BST iterators.
Always handle the `null` node as the base case **first**, or you dereference a null child.
Iterative inorder: push lefts onto a stack, pop to visit, then dive right. Stack depth is `O(h)`, not `O(n)`.
Recursion uses the call stack (`O(h)` hidden space); the iterative version makes that stack explicit so you control it.
whenToUse: You must process every node and the *order* of processing matters
Inorder specifically when the tree is a BST and you want values in sorted order
Preorder when you need to copy/serialize a tree top-down (root before children)
Postorder when a node's result depends on its children (heights, deletes, bottom-up DP)
antiSignals: You need nodes grouped *by level* → that's BFS / level-order, not DFS
You need the shortest path / minimum depth → BFS short-circuits earlier
Order genuinely doesn't matter → any traversal works; pick the simplest
remember.takeaway: Traversal is the alphabet of tree problems. Memorize that the three DFS orders differ only by the position of the visit, that inorder on a BST yields sorted output, and that an explicit stack converts any recursion into iteration. Almost every tree question is one of these walks with a tiny bit of bookkeeping bolted on.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can write a clean recursive tree walk, explain the difference between the three orders, and convert the recursion into an explicit-stack iterative version on request.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Mixing up inorder vs preorder ordering, forgetting the null base case, or being unable to produce the iterative version when the interviewer says 'now do it without recursion'.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name what each order is good for (preorder copies, postorder aggregates, inorder sorts a BST), then offer Morris traversal for O(1) space to show you know recursion isn't the only tool.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return the **inorder** traversal of its nodes' values.

Inorder means: recursively traverse the left subtree, visit the current node, then recursively traverse the right subtree. (Preorder and postorder are the natural variations the interviewer will ask you to produce next.)
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
Stretch: solve it in O(1) extra space (Morris traversal)
understanding: Produce the node values in a specific visiting order. The tree may be empty (return an empty list). The recursive solution is trivial; the entire interview value is in (a) knowing which order is which and (b) being able to remove recursion when asked.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which traversal order do you want — inorder, preorder, or postorder?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: LeetCode 94 asks for inorder, but stating that you can produce all three by moving one line shows mastery.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — node count can be 0. The traversal of an empty tree is an empty list, handled by the null base case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want recursive or iterative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lead with recursive (cleanest), then offer the explicit-stack iterative version since it's the standard follow-up.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is there any constraint on extra space?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Recursion is O(h) on the call stack. If they want O(1) extra space, pivot to Morris traversal which threads links temporarily.

examples.explanation: 1 has no left child. Visit 1, then its right subtree rooted at 2 whose left child is 3 → inorder of that subtree is 3,2. Combined: 1,3,2.
Left subtree of 1 (rooted at 2) inorder = 4,2,5; visit 1; right subtree (rooted at 3) inorder = 3,6. Concatenate: 4,2,5,1,3,6.

diagrams.title: Picking the right traversal
diagrams.caption: All three DFS orders differ only by where the visit happens; BFS is a different animal for level grouping.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS — All Three Orders
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. It's the cleanest, most readable solution and demonstrates you understand the recursive structure of a tree.
hints: A binary tree is recursive by definition: every node's left and right children are themselves binary trees. What's the simplest function that processes a node and then calls itself on the children?
Write a helper that takes a node, returns immediately if it's null (base case), then makes a recursive call on left and right with a `visit` step somewhere in between.
To switch between preorder, inorder, and postorder, you only move the single line that records `node.val` — before both recursive calls, between them, or after both.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n nodes is visited exactly once → O(n) time. The recursion depth equals the tree height h, so the call stack uses O(h) space — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree.
approaches.explanation:
A binary tree is defined recursively — a node plus a left subtree plus a right subtree — so the most natural traversal is itself recursive. The helper does exactly three things in some order: process the current node, recurse left, recurse right.

**The base case comes first.** Before touching `node.val` or its children, return immediately when `node` is null. An empty subtree contributes nothing to the traversal, and checking this first is what stops you from dereferencing a missing child.

**The three orders are one template.** Preorder records the value *before* descending (`node, left, right`); inorder records it *between* the two descents (`left, node, right`); postorder records it *after* both (`left, right, node`). That single moved line is the entire conceptual difference — interviewers love asking you to convert one to another precisely because it tests whether you understand the structure rather than memorized one snippet.

**Why each order exists.** Preorder visits a parent before its children, which is the order you need to *copy* or *serialize* a tree top-down. Postorder visits children before the parent, which is required whenever a node's answer depends on its subtrees — computing heights, deleting a tree, or bottom-up DP. Inorder on a binary *search* tree emits values in sorted ascending order, the property behind Validate BST, Kth Smallest, and in-order successors.

**Why O(n) is optimal.** You must look at every node to produce its value, so no traversal can beat linear time. The only thing you can optimize is the *space* — and that's exactly what the iterative and Morris variants attack.
approaches.insight: Don't memorize three separate functions — memorize one template and remember that the position of the `visit` line is the whole story. "Pre/in/post" literally describes when you visit relative to the recursion: PRE-before, IN-between, POST-after.

dryRun.input: root = [1,null,2,3] (1's right child is 2; 2's left child is 3)
dryRun.intro: Inorder = left, node, right. We follow the recursion and record a value only when we hit the 'node' step with the left side already done.

steps.action: left done (empty) → record 1, then go right
3's subtree done → record 2, right is null

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def inorderTraversal(self, root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    out: list[int] = []

    def inorder(node: TreeNode) -> None:
        if not node:                 # base case
            return
        inorder(node.left)           # left
        out.append(node.val)         # node
        inorder(node.right)          # right

    inorder(root)
    return out

# Preorder: put out.append(node.val) ABOVE inorder(node.left)
# Postorder: put out.append(node.val) BELOW inorder(node.right)

java.explanation: Base case FIRST — an empty subtree adds nothing and this prevents a null dereference on a missing child.
Fully traverse the left subtree before touching this node — that's the 'left' in left-node-right.
The visit. Its position is the ONLY thing that distinguishes in/pre/post order.

python.explanation: Base case — None means an empty subtree, return without recording anything.
Record the value between the two recursive calls — move this line to change the order.

pitfalls: Forgetting the null base case — recursing into a null child throws a NullPointerException / AttributeError.
Placing the visit line in the wrong spot and silently returning preorder when inorder was asked.
Building the result list as a return value and concatenating at every node — that's O(n) per merge, O(n²) total; pass a shared accumulator instead.

approaches.name: Iterative Inorder with an Explicit Stack (+ Morris)
approaches.whenToMention: The standard follow-up. Offer it the moment the interviewer says 'now without recursion', and mention Morris if they push for O(1) space.
hints: Recursion is just a stack the runtime manages for you. To remove recursion, manage that stack yourself — what would you push, and when?
Walk as far left as possible, pushing every node onto a stack. When you can't go left, the top of the stack is the next node to visit (its left subtree is exhausted).
After visiting a popped node, move to its right child and repeat the 'go all the way left' process. Loop until both the stack is empty and the current pointer is null.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every node is pushed and popped exactly once → O(n) time. The stack holds at most one full root-to-leaf path of nodes, so its size is bounded by the height h → O(h) space. Morris traversal drops this to O(1) by reusing null right-pointers as temporary threads.
approaches.explanation:
The recursive version hides a stack inside the language runtime. The iterative version makes that stack explicit so you control the memory and can run on trees deep enough to overflow the call stack.

**The core invariant.** Maintain a `curr` pointer and a stack. Repeatedly push `curr` and move to `curr.left` until `curr` is null — this stacks up an entire left spine. When you can go no further left, the node on top of the stack has *no unvisited left subtree*, so it's exactly the next inorder value: pop it, record it, then set `curr` to its right child and repeat. The loop ends only when both the stack is empty and `curr` is null.

**Why this produces inorder specifically.** A node is recorded only after its whole left subtree has been pushed and drained. Then we pivot to the right subtree. That's the literal definition of left-node-right. Preorder iterative is simpler (push right then left, visit on pop); postorder iterative usually needs two stacks or a 'last visited' marker — worth mentioning but not worth writing unless asked.

**Morris traversal — the O(1) flex.** Recursion and an explicit stack both cost O(h) space. Morris traversal achieves O(1) extra space by temporarily rewiring the tree: for each node with a left child, find that left subtree's rightmost node (the inorder predecessor) and point its null right pointer back to the current node, creating a temporary 'thread' that lets you climb back up without a stack. On the second visit you tear the thread down, restoring the tree. It's O(n) time still (each edge is traversed at most twice) and a genuine standout answer — but state the trade-off: it mutates the tree mid-traversal, so it's risky in concurrent or read-only settings.
approaches.insight: Any recursive traversal can be made iterative by simulating the call stack with an explicit `Stack`/list. The trick that makes interviewers nod is articulating the invariant out loud — 'a node is on the stack while its left subtree is still being processed' — rather than just reciting the loop.

dryRun.intro: curr starts at root. Push lefts until null, pop to visit, then go right. Stack shown top-first.

code.python:
def inorderTraversal(self, root: TreeNode) -> list[int]:
    out: list[int] = []
    stack: list[TreeNode] = []
    curr = root
    while curr or stack:
        while curr:                   # dive to the leftmost node
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left
        curr = stack.pop()            # leftmost unvisited node
        out.append(curr.val)          # visit it
        curr = curr.right             # then explore its right subtree
    return out

java.explanation: Keep going while there is a node to descend into OR nodes waiting on the stack to be visited.
Push the entire left spine — every node here still has an unprocessed left subtree.
Top of stack has no remaining left subtree → it's the next inorder node.
Visit happens right after the pop — left is done, node now, right next.
Pivot to the right subtree and repeat the dive-left process.

python.explanation: Continue while there's a node to descend OR pending nodes on the stack.
Push the whole left spine onto the stack.
Leftmost unvisited node — its left subtree is exhausted.
Record the value, satisfying left-node order.
Move to the right child to continue inorder.

edgeCases.behavior: curr starts null and stack is empty, so the while condition is false immediately → returns [].
Push 1, inner loop ends, pop and visit 1, right is null → returns [1].
Stack fills to depth = height (O(n) here); nodes pop in order 1,2,3 — the iterative version still uses O(h) space, which degrades to O(n) on a degenerate tree.

pitfalls: Visiting a node when you push it instead of when you pop it — that yields preorder, not inorder.
Forgetting to move to curr.right after the pop, causing an infinite loop or missed right subtrees.
Reaching for Morris traversal in a concurrent or read-only context — it temporarily mutates the tree's pointers.

commonMistakes: Confusing the orders — recording the node before recursing left when inorder was requested.
Omitting the null base case, causing a crash on a missing child or an empty tree.
Visiting on push (preorder) when writing the iterative inorder, instead of visiting on pop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong visit position (preorder when inorder asked)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The three orders share the same recursion skeleton, so a single misplaced line silently returns the wrong order. For [1,null,2,3], preorder gives [1,2,3] but inorder must give [1,3,2].

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Visiting on push in the iterative version
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you record the value when you push the node onto the stack, you emit it before its left subtree — that's preorder. Inorder requires recording only when you pop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Concatenating subtree lists at every node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Returning a new list per node and concatenating (left + [val] + right) copies O(n) elements at upper levels, degrading to O(n²). Pass a single shared accumulator instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
out = []
def inorder(node):
    if not node:
        return
    inorder(node.left)
    out.append(node.val)
    inorder(node.right)

followupVariations.title: Binary Tree Preorder Traversal
followupVariations.hint: Same template — move the visit before both recursive calls; iterative version pushes right child then left.

followupVariations.title: Binary Tree Postorder Traversal
followupVariations.hint: Visit after both children; iterative trick is to do a reversed preorder (node,right,left) and reverse the output.

followupVariations.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
followupVariations.hint: Switch from DFS to BFS — use a queue and process one level per outer-loop iteration.

followupVariations.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
followupVariations.hint: Inorder on a BST is sorted — stop after popping the kth node in the iterative inorder.

patternNote: Depth-first traversal is the foundational tree pattern. Recognise it whenever you must touch every node in a defined order. Postorder for bottom-up aggregation (heights, sums), preorder for top-down construction (copy, serialize), inorder for sorted BST output. The explicit-stack conversion and Morris traversal are the space-optimization layers on top.
